**Common side effects of aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)** | Category | Typical side effects | Notes | |----------|----------------------|-------| | **Gastro‑intestinal (GI)** | • Stomach upset, heartburn, nausea, vomiting
• Gastric irritation or gastritis
• Peptic ulcer disease
• GI bleeding (can be occult or obvious) | Aspirin inhibits CO‑X‑1, which reduces protective prostaglandins in the stomach lining. Taking it with food, using enteric‑coated tablets, or pairing it with a proton‑pump inhibitor (PPI) can lower the risk. | | **Bleeding / Hematologic** | • Prolonged bleeding time
• Easy bruising
• Nosebleeds (epistaxis)
• Gastrointestinal or intracranial hemorrhage (rare, but serious) | The antiplatelet effect is why aspirin is used for cardiovascular protection, but it also makes bleeding more likely. | | **Ear‑related** | • Tinnitus (ringing in the ears)
• Hearing loss (usually reversible) | Usually occurs at higher doses (≥ 3 g/day). | | **Allergic / Dermatologic** | • Rash, itching, urticaria
• Angio‑edema (swelling of lips, face, throat)
• Anaphylaxis (very rare) | People with asthma, nasal polyps, or a history of aspirin‑sensitive asthma may develop “aspirin‑exacerbated respiratory disease” (AERD). | | **Renal** | • Decreased kidney function or acute kidney injury (especially in volume‑depleted patients) | More common in the elderly or those taking other nephrotoxic drugs. | | **Metabolic / Miscellaneous** | • Mild fever, chills
• Hyperventilation (rare) | Generally uncommon. | ### Tips to reduce side‑effect risk 1. **Take with food or a full glass of water** – helps protect the stomach lining. 2. **Use the lowest effective dose** – low‑dose (81 mg) aspirin is usually enough for cardiovascular prophylaxis and carries fewer GI risks. 3. **Consider enteric‑coated or buffered formulations** – they dissolve farther down the GI tract. 4. **Avoid alcohol, NSAIDs, or steroids** while on aspirin, as they increase GI bleeding risk. 5. **Discuss with a clinician** before starting aspirin if you have: - A history of peptic ulcers or GI bleeding - Chronic kidney disease - Uncontrolled asthma or known aspirin allergy - Upcoming surgery or dental procedures (you may need to stop aspirin temporarily). > **Important:** This information is for general educational purposes and is **not** a substitute for professional medical advice. Always consult your healthcare provider before starting, stopping, or changing the dose of aspirin.
